record.title: The Headache That Made History: How Lou Gehrig Became the Iron Horse
record.summary: On June 2, 1925, a routine lineup change turned into one of baseball's defining streaks.
record.text:
It started with a headache. On June 2, 1925, New York Yankees first baseman Wally Pipp told manager Miller Huggins he wasn't feeling well and asked out of the lineup. Huggins turned to his bench and picked a 21-year-old named Henry Louis Gehrig, who'd pinch-hit the day before against Walter Johnson and flied out.

Gehrig started that afternoon, batting sixth against the Washington Senators. He went 3-for-5 and scored a run in an 8-5 Yankees win. Nobody in the ballpark that day had any reason to think it was historic. Pipp would try to get his job back more than once over the following weeks, but Gehrig never left the lineup again -- not for 2,130 consecutive games, a streak that ran until April 30, 1939, and stood as the major-league record for 56 years, until Cal Ripken Jr. broke it in 1995.

What made the streak remarkable wasn't just its length. Gehrig played through fractures, back spasms, and the kind of everyday soreness that ends most careers early, all without missing a start -- a durability that earned him the nickname "The Iron Horse." The June 2 lineup card is a small, almost forgettable piece of paper. But it marks the exact moment an ordinary substitution became the start of one of the sport's most enduring legends.

record.title: The Luckiest Man on the Face of the Earth
record.summary: On July 4, 1939, a packed Yankee Stadium heard Lou Gehrig say goodbye.
record.text:
Gehrig played his last game on April 30, 1939, brought down not by age but by amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The Yankees held Lou Gehrig Appreciation Day that July 4th, and a crowd of 61,808 packed the stadium between games of a doubleheader.

Gehrig stood silent at first, too moved to speak, until the crowd's chants of "We want Gehrig!" pulled him back to the microphone. What followed became one of the most quoted speeches in sports history: "Fans, for the past two weeks you have been reading about the bad break I got. Yet today I consider myself the luckiest man on the face of the earth." He was gone less than two years later, but that afternoon is still how most people remember him.

record.title: A Rule Broken Once: Gehrig's Special Election to Cooperstown
record.summary: The Hall of Fame waived its own waiting period for Gehrig -- something it's done only twice, ever.
record.text: Hall of Fame eligibility normally requires years of waiting after a career ends. On December 7, 1939 -- just 221 days after Gehrig played his final game -- the Baseball Writers' Association of America voted unanimously to suspend that rule and elect him immediately. It remains one of only two special elections in the Hall's history; the other came after Roberto Clemente's death in 1972. The gesture said plainly what the record book already showed: there was no reason to wait.

record.title: Before the Pinstripes: Gehrig's One Afternoon at Columbia
record.summary: A scout's train ride to a college doubleheader changed baseball history.
record.text: Before he was a Yankee, Gehrig was an engineering student at Columbia University on a football scholarship. On April 18, 1923 -- the same day Yankee Stadium opened across town -- he struck out 17 batters pitching for Columbia against Williams College, a school record that still stands. Word reached Yankees scout Paul Krichell, who came to see him play against Rutgers days later and left convinced. Krichell signed Gehrig to a $1,500 contract, and on June 15, 1923, the future Iron Horse made his major-league debut as a pinch hitter -- the quiet start of a career that would define an era.
